design_detail: Mini review (the authors' term; the format was chosen instead of a systematic review for concision and timeliness) of protective behavioural strategies (PBS: harm-reduction strategies used by the individual) for non-clinical use of classical psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin) and of MDMA and ketamine. Search: PubMed and Google Scholar, English, 2006 to 2023, four phrases combining psychedelic or hallucinogen with protective behavioral strategies or harm reduction, plus the reference lists of the articles found. No inclusion or exclusion criteria, no count of records screened or included, no appraisal of the cited studies and no quantitative synthesis. Strategies are arranged by time (before, during and after a psychedelic experience) in Table 1, which names 17 distinct sources (editors' count), followed by sections on measuring strategies and on associations with outcomes (four studies). 65 references.
can_establish: Which individual-level strategies for non-clinical use of psychedelics, MDMA and ketamine the authors found described in the literature from 2006 to 2023, arranged by before, during and after use, and how little outcome research they could find.
cannot_establish: Whether any strategy reduces harm or improves the experience (nothing is appraised, and the outcome evidence cited is one cross-sectional survey, one scale study, one ketamine study whose design the review does not state and one unreviewed preprint scoping review); how often strategies are used; or whether the catalogue is complete (four search phrases, no stated selection criteria, and the authors say articles may have been left out for space).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Literature found through PubMed and Google Scholar (English, 2006 to 2023; 2006 taken as the start of the 'psychedelic renaissance') with four search phrases and the reference lists of the articles found (Method, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated beyond language, years, non-clinical contexts and the drug classes covered (classical psychedelics, MDMA, ketamine). Books, a practitioner handbook and two preprints are cited alongside peer-reviewed studies.
sample.selection_effects: Two search engines, one of them (Google Scholar) not reproducible; four narrow phrases, which the authors concede will miss studies describing the same strategies in other words (Limitations, 1st paragraph); no flow of records; selection by the authors without stated criteria, and the authors note pertinent articles may have been omitted for space. Much of the cited material is qualitative (open-ended survey questions, analyses of online forums and trip reports) or self-rated helpfulness.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The strategies come from the cited studies: qualitative interviews and open-ended questions, content analyses of an online forum (Reddit r/psychonaut) and of trip reports (Erowid), checklists in online surveys, a new scale (Protective Strategies for Psychedelics Scale) and a survey of callers to a peer-support helpline.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. Table 1 names seven strategies concerning the amount taken, drug checking and combinations as strategies reported in the literature; the review tests none and gives no amounts, and this card reproduces none.
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed only as a strategy category (care with, or avoidance of, some combinations) and as a reported practice (using cannabis alongside psychedelics was itself reported as a strategy in Carbonaro et al., 2016, as cited). Combinations are outside this card's scope and belong to the interactions page.

comparison.controls: None at review level. In the four outcome studies discussed, comparisons are between people reporting more or fewer strategies (Palmer and Maynard, 2022, a survey; Vidal Giné et al., 2016, design not stated in the review), across levels of a preparedness scale (McAlpine et al.), or within a preprint scoping review (Edwards et al., 2022), as summarized.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed. The review does not discuss that people who use more strategies may differ from people who use fewer in experience, intentions, setting, substance, amount or mental health, any of which could explain an association with outcomes.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: the Challenging Experience Questionnaire (26 items) and the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (6 items) in Palmer and Maynard (2022); unnamed mental-health and wellbeing measures after the experience in the Psychedelic Preparedness Scale study (McAlpine et al.); ketamine-related adverse outcomes and overall harm in Vidal Giné et al. (2016); perceived helpfulness in Carbonaro et al. (2016), McCartney et al. (2023) and the Fireside Project caller survey (Pleet et al., 2023).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed; the review calls for the development and validation of measures of strategies and of outcomes (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Consequences', 'harm' and 'risk reduction' are not defined at review level and take whatever meaning each cited study gave them. Several of the cited findings are perceived effectiveness rated by the people who used the strategy.

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled or computed. Second-hand figures only: 91% of respondents in Carbonaro et al. (2016) used at least one strategy during a challenging experience with psilocybin mushrooms and rated the strategies only modestly effective; 65.9% of surveyed Fireside Project callers (April 2021 to September 2022) found the helpline helpful in de-escalating distress; Palmer and Maynard (2022), n = 163, strategy use positively associated with emotional breakthrough and negatively with challenging experiences (no coefficients given in the review).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration; the authors chose a mini-review format instead of a systematic one (Introduction, 4th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The summary of Palmer and Maynard (2022) omits that the association with challenging experiences was not statistically significant for the most recent experience and that the predictor was a score weighted by participants' importance ratings, not a count (see reporting issues). All MDMA strategy-outcome statements rest on a rapid scoping review posted as a preprint, which the review does not identify as unreviewed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A catalogue of strategies described in mostly qualitative and self-report literature: sourcing, amounts, checking and combinations, mindset and intentions, the physical place and the company, telling a trusted person of one's plans, rest, exercise, water and a meal beforehand, calming, grounding, music, changing the setting and calling on others during difficult moments, a peer-support helpline, and integration afterwards. The review reports disagreement in the literature on the best place, on whom to be with, and on sober sitters. For outcomes it found one cross-sectional survey of classical psychedelic use (163 people), one preparedness-scale study (drug class not stated), one ketamine study (design not stated) and one preprint scoping review on MDMA; for perceived helpfulness, a mushroom survey (strategies rated modestly effective) and a helpline survey.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says emerging evidence suggests that psychedelic PBS use may be associated with decreased consequences, and the Implications say the review may give community members initial insights into risk mitigation. The wording is hedged and the conclusion asks for research on efficacy, but: (1) the 'emerging evidence' pools classical psychedelics with ketamine and MDMA, and for classical psychedelics rests on one retrospective cross-sectional survey and one scale study; (2) the introduction asserts the "efficacy of PBS in reducing consequences associated with alcohol and cannabis use" (Introduction, 3rd paragraph) on four references that, by their titles, are a scale-development paper, a review of measures and associated interventions, and two moderator studies, none a trial by title; (3) Table 1 presents the strategies as a list that can be read as recommendations, with only a table note saying that their support varies; (4) the summary of the main outcome study overstates its result (reporting issue 1). Against this, the authors mark their own inferences ('we posit'), state that few studies have examined outcomes, and name the limits of the mini-review format.

timeline.event: Carbonaro et al. survey of challenging experiences after psilocybin mushrooms: 91% used strategies during the experience and rated them only modestly effective (as cited).
Vidal Giné et al. study of patterns of use, strategies and harms among people who use ketamine recreationally (as cited; the review does not state its design).
Palmer and Maynard cross-sectional survey of 163 people recalling their first and most recent psychedelic experiences: the review's main outcome study for classical psychedelics
Simonsson et al. survey of challenging experiences, cited for avoiding use after a major life event
Mian et al. develop the Protective Strategies for Psychedelics Scale (32 items, two factors), not yet tested against challenging experiences (as cited).
Pleet et al. survey of callers to the Fireside Project peer-support line: 65.9% found it helpful in de-escalating distress (as cited).
McAlpine et al. Psychedelic Preparedness Scale (dated 2023 in the review's text, 2024 in its reference list): higher preparedness went with better mental health and wellbeing afterwards (as cited).
Wood, McAlpine and Kamboj mixed-methods study of strategies for resolving challenging experiences (not cited by this review)
Dutton et al. scoping review of harm-reduction practices for people who use psychedelics (on this project's interactions list; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: A map of strategies named in the literature, not evidence that any of them works. No prospective or experimental test of a strategy for classical psychedelics is cited. Palmer and Maynard (2022) has its own card and should be cited directly instead of through this review; the MDMA statements should be checked against the published version of the Edwards et al. scoping review, if one exists; later reviews on this project's lists (Dutton et al., 2025) may supersede this one.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people planning non-clinical psychedelic use that records the strategies planned and used before and during the experience, the substance, amount, place and company, and rates the experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire, need for help, lasting difficulties) within days, with adjustment for prior experience and intentions; for a single strategy with plausible benefit, such as access to peer support or structured preparation material, a randomized offer of that support.

domains.note: Two engines (one not reproducible), four narrow phrases, English 2006 to 2023 and reference-list searching are stated; but there are no inclusion criteria, no record flow and no count of included studies, and the authors say relevant articles may be missing because of terminology and space.

No appraisal. Cross-sectional surveys, qualitative studies, forum and trip-report analyses, books, a handbook and two preprints are cited alike, and self-rated helpfulness is reported without saying that it is self-rated.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the cited strategy or outcome studies is by the authors.

The authors flag their own inferences and the Table 1 note says support varies, but the introduction asserts the efficacy of alcohol and cannabis strategies without trial evidence, and the main outcome study is summarized as fewer challenging experiences with more strategies.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on whether strategies help (null and unfavourable findings under-represented)
domains.note: Some caveats are given (false security from trusted sources; inexperienced sitters may harm the experience; ketamine testing and having a sober person present not associated with outcomes; supplements taken before or after MDMA poorly supported and possibly harmful), but the non-significant result for the most recent experience in Palmer and Maynard and the modest perceived effectiveness in Carbonaro et al. do not reach the abstract.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3), so the editors' checklist is used. The search is described but narrow, selection is unstated and nothing is appraised; the overall judgment cannot be milder than the worst domain. Cite the review only as a map of the strategies named in the literature up to 2023 and for the observation that outcome research on them is scarce. Do not cite it for any strategy reducing harm or improving experiences: cite the primary studies (Palmer and Maynard, 2022, has its own card), and say that the MDMA statements come second-hand from an unreviewed preprint. A claim resting only on this review stays at draft (METHODS §6.3).

key_findings.finding: Method: PubMed and Google Scholar searched for English-language articles from 2006 to 2023 with four phrases combining psychedelic or hallucinogen with protective behavioral strategies or harm reduction, plus the reference lists of the articles found; classical psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin) and non-classical ones (MDMA, ketamine) in non-clinical contexts. A mini-review format was chosen instead of a systematic one for a concise, timely summary.
key_findings.locator: Method, 1st paragraph; Introduction, 4th paragraph; Abstract › Method

key_findings.finding: The authors found that most research on psychedelic protective strategies used qualitative methods (open-ended questions about harm-reduction practices, analyses of online drug forums) and describe a culture of harm reduction in psychedelic communities, illustrated by a content analysis of the Reddit r/psychonaut forum.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patterns of psychedelic PBS use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Table 1 arranges the strategies by time. Before use: drug acquisition (2 strategies), amounts, drug checking and combinations (7), set and setting (6: setting intentions, reflecting on motives, cultivating a positive mindset, avoiding use in negative or unstable moods, choosing the physical space, choosing the social setting), planning for challenging experiences (1: telling a trusted person of one's plans), bodily nourishment (4: rest, exercise, hydration, a nutritious meal). During use: working through challenging experiences (8: meditating, changing the physical or social setting, calming audio, calling on sitters or guides, grounding in nature, trying to calm the mind, moving the body, a peer-support helpline). After use: integration (4 examples). 17 distinct sources are named (editors' count). The table note says these are strategies proposed in the literature with varying support and some mixed findings.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and its note; Results › Patterns of psychedelic PBS use, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Drug acquisition: buying from reputable sources such as a trusted friend is described as one widely identified acquisition strategy; the review notes that it may give a false sense of security that leads people to skip testing, that cryptomarket purchasing was described as risk reduction in a field study of the Silk Road market, and that producing or foraging one's own supply is not feasible for every substance and carries more legal risk.
key_findings.locator: Results › Before the psychedelic experience: Preparation PBS › Drug acquisition, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Strategies about amounts, drug checking (reagent kits, fentanyl test strips), weighing and combinations are reported in the cited surveys and forum studies; the review notes that they vary by substance (adulterants more common in powders and tablets than in plant material, and mushroom weight varying with curing, as cited) and that using cannabis alongside psychedelics has itself been reported as a strategy (Carbonaro et al., 2016, as cited). No amounts are tested or given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Before the psychedelic experience: Preparation PBS › Dosing, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Set and setting: mindset strategies centre on setting intentions (reflecting on motives, cultivating a positive mindset, avoiding use in negative or unstable moods) and also include meeting obligations first and choosing the timing, for example not after a major life event and keeping the next day free (citing Mian et al., 2023, and Simonsson et al., 2023). The review finds no consensus on the place (home versus a festival, for example) or the company (alone, a sitter, friends): spaces that feel comfortable and safe are generally recommended, and while some evidence stresses a sober sitter, inexperienced sitters can harm the experience through unsupportive behaviour (Engel et al., 2022, as cited).
key_findings.locator: Results › Curating an optimal set and setting › Mind set, Selecting a physical setting and Deciding who to trip with, one paragraph each

key_findings.finding: Planning and the body: people report telling a trusted person of their plans and asking them to be available if a challenging experience or emergency arises (Engel et al., 2022, as cited), and some researchers speculate that planning eases anxiety beforehand; preparation of the body includes rest, exercise, hydration and a nutritious meal before use, while fasting before some psychedelics is also discussed in the literature (Palmer and Maynard, 2022, as cited).
key_findings.locator: Results › Planning for challenging experiences, 1st paragraph; Bodily nourishment, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: During use: in a thematic analysis of 22 Erowid trip reports covering ketamine, MDMA, psilocybin and LSD (McCartney et al., 2023), grounding in nature and listening to music were reported as ways to ease negative states during challenging experiences; perceived efficacy differed by substance (nature more for MDMA, music more for ketamine, more variable and dependent on the individual for psilocybin and LSD).
key_findings.locator: Results › During the psychedelic experience: PBS for working through challenging experiences, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: In a survey of challenging experiences after psilocybin mushrooms (Carbonaro et al., 2016), 91% of respondents used strategies to mitigate the experience (calming the mind, changing the physical setting, moving the body, changing the social environment, asking a friend for help, using cannabis or other drugs) and perceived them as only modestly effective.
key_findings.locator: Results › During the psychedelic experience: PBS for working through challenging experiences, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The Fireside Project psychedelic peer-support line, set up in 2020: in a survey of callers between April 2021 and September 2022, 65.9% of respondents perceived it as helpful in de-escalating their distress (Pleet et al., 2023, as cited; response rate and denominator not given in the review).
key_findings.locator: Results › During the psychedelic experience: PBS for working through challenging experiences, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Integration after use is variably defined; Bathje et al. (2022) identified 14 integration themes in the literature. The review suggests that inadequate integration could contribute to extended difficulties such as derealization or panic attacks, citing a 2023 SSRN preprint (Evans et al.).
key_findings.locator: Results › After the psychedelic experience: Integration-related PBS, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Measurement: the Protective Strategies for Psychedelics Scale (Mian et al., 2023) has 32 items in two factors (short-term and long-term strategies) from principal components analysis, showed convergent validity with alcohol and cannabis protective-strategy measures and a moderate association with lifetime psychedelic use, and had not been examined against challenging experiences when the review was written.
key_findings.locator: Results › Measuring psychedelic PBS use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Main outcome study for classical psychedelics, as summarized: Palmer and Maynard (2022), cross-sectional, n = 163, strategy use for the first and most recent experience from a list of 28; strategy use positively associated with Emotional Breakthrough Inventory scores and negatively with Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores, read by the review as more strategies going with more breakthroughs and fewer challenging experiences.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Checked against the source (PMC9310449; card sc_palmer_2022): the predictor was a sum of practices weighted by mean importance ratings, not a count; the CEQ correlation was significant for the first experience only (r = −0.21; most recent r = −0.15, p = 0.061); the size of the list is not stated in the source's main text.

key_findings.finding: McAlpine et al. (Psychedelic Preparedness Scale; subdomains Knowledge-Expectations, Intention-Preparation, Psychophysical-Readiness and Support-Planning): people with higher preparedness before a psychedelic experience scored significantly higher on mental health and wellbeing measures afterwards (as summarized; no figures, design or sample given in the review).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ketamine (Vidal Giné et al., 2016, as summarized): three strategies about how often and how much ketamine was used, and a fourth, avoiding mixing it with other drugs, were negatively associated with ketamine-related adverse outcomes, while testing the ketamine and having a sober person in the group were not; people who used strategies more often reported less harm overall.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: MDMA, from a rapid scoping review posted as a preprint (Edwards et al., 2022): taking breaks to avoid overheating at dance events, keeping hydrated, avoiding certain combinations, moderating consumption and not using alone are described as associated with risk reduction; taking supplements or medicines before or after use to prevent unwanted effects ('pre-loading' and 'post-loading') was poorly supported and potentially harmful, with 5-HTP named as a possible serotonin-syndrome risk alongside MDMA (Silins et al., 2007, as cited).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Reference 48 is a Research Square preprint (DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-2178425/v1); these statements are second-hand from an unreviewed source.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the mini-review format simplifies issues and may omit pertinent articles for space; empirical studies are few; the search was limited to English-language articles from 2006 to 2023; and inconsistent terminology may have excluded relevant evidence.

Conclusion: many people who use psychedelics employ protective strategies; research on the efficacy of specific strategies is needed so that harm-reduction recommendations are evidence-based, with attention to which strategies work for whom. The authors call for rigorous cross-sectional, longitudinal and experimental studies and for measures developed with people with lived experience.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary of Palmer and Maynard (2022) departs from the source in four ways: it says the practice list came from online forums and the literature, while the source names trusted online harm-reduction resources, the literature and discussion with colleagues; it gives the list as 28 strategies, a number not stated in the source's main text; it describes the source's example of an anecdotal myth (drinking orange juice) as aimed at enhancing the experience, while the source gives it as a belief that it lowers the chance of a bad trip; and it reads the result as more strategies going with fewer challenging experiences, while the source's predictor was an importance-weighted score and the challenging-experience correlation was not statistically significant for the most recent experience (r = −0.15, p = 0.061). Within the review itself, the CEQ is defined as a scale of distress during an experience, yet a lower score is read as 'fewer challenging experiences'.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 1st paragraph; checked against PMC9310449 (Methods › Measures › Harm reduction practices; Results › Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The review makes the only classical-psychedelic outcome study look stronger and more uniform than it is; claims must cite Palmer and Maynard directly (card sc_palmer_2022).

reporting_issues.issue: Inconsistent years for the same sources: Pestana et al. is 2020 in Table 1 and reference 26 but 2021 in the Drug acquisition text; Bathje et al. is 2023 in Table 1 and its note but 2022 in the integration text and reference 52; McAlpine et al. is 2023 in the text but 2024 in reference 57.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 and note; Results › Drug acquisition, 2nd paragraph; Integration-related PBS, 1st paragraph; Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 2nd paragraph; references 26, 52, 57
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; match sources by reference number and DOI, not by author-year.

reporting_issues.issue: Two preprints are cited as evidence without being identified as such: Edwards et al. (2022), a rapid scoping review on Research Square (reference 48), is the only source for every MDMA strategy-outcome statement and appears in Table 1; Evans et al. (2023), an SSRN preprint (reference 53), supports the statement that poor integration could give rise to extended difficulties.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 4th paragraph; Integration-related PBS, 1st paragraph; references 48 and 53
reporting_issues.consequence: The MDMA findings are second-hand from an unreviewed source; the published versions, if any, must be read before these statements are used.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction states that protective strategies are efficacious in reducing consequences of alcohol and cannabis use, citing references 13, 16, 18 and 19, which by their titles are the development of a strategies survey (Martens et al., 2005), a review of strategy measures and associated PBS-related interventions (Peterson et al., 2021) and two studies of the independent and moderating effects of marijuana strategies (Pearson et al., 2019; Bravo et al., 2017); by title, none is a trial of a strategy.
reporting_issues.consequence: As cited, the efficacy statement is asserted rather than shown in this review; whether the review of interventions (reference 16) supports it would need that review to be read. For alcohol, Pearson (2013), a critical review on this round's list, is the source to check: it finds mixed evidence that strategies change drinking.
